feed.title: Monocurl Essays
feed.subtitle: Free visual lessons in algebra, geometry, trigonometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, physics and more. Every idea is drawn and animated, and every figure's source is open.

entry.title: Why is a negative times a negative positive?
entry.summary: Multiplying by a negative number flips the number line about zero, and two flips cancel. We see it, then prove it from the distributive law.

entry.title: The distributive law as a picture: FOIL and (a+b)²
entry.summary: Cutting a rectangle into pieces explains FOIL, why (a+b)² has a middle term 2ab, and why (a+b)(a−b) = a² − b². Each identity is then proved.

entry.title: Completing the square and the quadratic formula
entry.summary: Solve x² + 6x = 16 by rearranging a square and a rectangle into a bigger square with one corner missing, then turn that picture into the quadratic formula.

entry.title: What slope means, and why y = mx + b is a line
entry.summary: A phone bill that grows by the same amount per gigabyte plots as a straight line. Similar triangles explain why, and give slope and y = mx + b their meaning.

entry.title: Solving two equations at once: where lines meet
entry.summary: Ten heads and 28 legs: how many chickens and rabbits? Each clue is a line of possibilities, and elimination pivots a line about the point where they cross.

entry.title: Why x⁰ = 1, and negative and fractional exponents
entry.summary: Powers of 2 halve as the exponent drops, and one rule, add exponents when you multiply, forces 2⁰ = 1, 2⁻¹ = 1/2 and 2^(1/2) = √2.

entry.title: Absolute value is distance: solving |x − a| < r
entry.summary: Read |x − 3| < 2 as "x is within 2 of 3" and the answer, 1 < x < 5, can be seen on a number line. Also why multiplying by a negative flips an inequality.

entry.title: Why the angles of a triangle add to 180°
entry.summary: Tear the corners off any triangle and they line up along a straight edge. A single parallel line explains why, and a sphere shows the line is needed.

entry.title: The Pythagorean theorem: a proof you can see
entry.summary: Why the squares on the two short sides of a right triangle add up to the square on the long side, proved by moving four triangles inside a box.

entry.title: Why the area of a circle is πr²
entry.summary: The number π is defined by the distance around a circle. Cutting the circle into sectors, and then into rings, shows why the same π gives its area.

entry.title: Similar triangles and why area grows as the square
entry.summary: Scaling multiplies every length by one factor and keeps every angle. That explains shadows, maps, and why a pizza twice as wide is four times the pizza.

entry.title: The inscribed angle theorem and Thales' semicircle
entry.summary: From every point on one arc of a circle, a chord is seen under the same angle, half the angle at the center. Two isosceles triangles explain why.

entry.title: Why a cone is a third of a cylinder, and a sphere's volume
entry.summary: A cone holds exactly one third of the cylinder around it. A cube cut into three pyramids shows why, and the same slicing idea gives the volume of a sphere.

entry.title: The unit circle: sine and cosine as coordinates
entry.summary: Sine and cosine start as ratios in a right triangle, which stops at 90°. Placing the triangle in a circle of radius 1 extends them to every angle.

entry.title: Radians: measuring an angle by the arc it cuts
entry.summary: A radian is the angle whose arc is as long as the radius. With it, arc length, sector area and the rule sin θ ≈ θ need no conversion constants.

entry.title: Pythagorean identity: why sin² + cos² = 1
entry.summary: The identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 is the Pythagorean theorem on the unit circle. Tangent and secant are lengths in the same picture and give two more.

entry.title: Angle addition formulas: sin(a + b) from one picture
entry.summary: The sine of a sum is not the sum of the sines. Two stacked right triangles show what it is, and a rotated chord proves the formulas for every angle.

entry.title: Law of cosines and law of sines: solving any triangle
entry.summary: The law of cosines is the Pythagorean theorem corrected for angles other than 90°. With the law of sines it solves any triangle, two-answer case included.

entry.title: Sine waves: amplitude, frequency and phase
entry.summary: A sine wave is the height of a point on a turning wheel. Amplitude, frequency and phase change the wheel, and explain how two waves add, cancel or beat.

entry.title: Shifting and stretching graphs: why f(x - 2) moves right
entry.summary: Adding 2 outside a function lifts its graph, but subtracting 2 inside moves it right. A graph is a set of points, and tracking one point explains why.

entry.title: Compound interest and where e comes from
entry.summary: Pay 100% interest in more and more instalments and a dollar grows to 2, 2.25, 2.44, 2.61, and then stops short of 2.72. That ceiling is the number e.

entry.title: What a logarithm is: turning multiplication into addition
entry.summary: A logarithm answers "what exponent gives this number?". Because exponents add when powers multiply, logarithms turn every product into a sum.

entry.title: Complex numbers: why multiplying by i is a quarter turn
entry.summary: No number on the line squares to -1. Read multiplication by -1 as a half turn and the missing number appears: a quarter turn, which needs a second axis.

entry.title: Euler's formula: why e^(iπ) = -1
entry.summary: You cannot multiply e by itself iπ times, so the famous equation needs a definition first. Compound interest supplies one, and it leads around a circle.

entry.title: Geometric series, and why 0.999... equals 1
entry.summary: What it means to add infinitely many numbers, when a geometric series has a sum, the formula a/(1 - r) with proof, and why 0.999... is exactly 1.

entry.title: Roots, factors and the shape of a polynomial
entry.summary: A cubic crosses the x axis once or three times, never exactly twice. The factor theorem, multiplicity and the leading term explain why, with proofs.

entry.title: What is a derivative? Speed at a single instant
entry.summary: A falling ball has a speed at every instant, but an instant is too short to measure a speed over. The derivative is the precise idea that resolves this.

entry.title: Why the derivative of x² is 2x: the power rule from pictures
entry.summary: A growing square gains two thin strips and a tiny corner. That picture explains the 2 in 2x, and counting the same pieces in general proves the power rule.

entry.title: The product rule and the chain rule, seen
entry.summary: A rectangle whose sides both change explains the product rule, and a nudge passed along a chain of number lines explains the chain rule. Both are then proved.

entry.title: Why the derivative of sine is cosine
entry.summary: Nudge a point around the unit circle and a tiny triangle appears, similar to the big one. Its legs are the derivatives of sine and cosine.

entry.title: What is a limit? The epsilon-delta definition, explained
entry.summary: A limit is a game. You name a tolerance, I answer with a window. From that one definition we prove the limit laws and the squeeze theorem.

entry.title: What is an integral? Adding up to get area
entry.summary: Distance from a changing speed, found by slicing time into pieces and adding. The definite integral is the limit of those sums, defined precisely and computed.

entry.title: The fundamental theorem of calculus, explained and proved
entry.summary: Why area and slope undo each other. The rate at which an area grows is the height of the curve, and that turns every integral into a subtraction.

entry.title: Taylor series: building functions out of polynomials
entry.summary: How a calculator finds cos(0.3) with only addition and multiplication, why factorials appear, how large the error can be, and where the method breaks.

entry.title: Maxima and minima: where the slope is zero
entry.summary: To fence the largest field or make the cheapest can, look where the derivative is zero, and also at the ends. Why that works, and when it does not.

entry.title: What is a vector? Arrows, lists of numbers, and adding them
entry.summary: A vector is a list of numbers read as a movement. Adding entry by entry matches placing arrows tip to tail, and two non-parallel arrows reach the whole plane.

entry.title: A matrix is a transformation of space
entry.summary: A 2x2 matrix moves every point of the plane, and its two columns say where the basis arrows land. Linearity is why those four numbers settle everything else.

entry.title: Why matrix multiplication is defined the way it is
entry.summary: Multiplying matrices means doing one transformation after another. The rows-times-columns rule, the failure of AB = BA and associativity all follow from that.

entry.title: The determinant is how much area gets scaled
entry.summary: A matrix multiplies every area in the plane by one number, ad - bc. That explains its sign, why det(AB) = det(A)det(B), and which matrices can be undone.

entry.title: The dot product: projection, angle and why the formula works
entry.summary: Multiply matching coordinates and add. The result measures how far one arrow reaches along another, which gives angles, projections and Cauchy-Schwarz.

entry.title: Eigenvectors: the directions a transformation leaves alone
entry.summary: Most arrows are knocked off their line by a matrix. The few that are only stretched are its eigenvectors, and they turn matrix powers into powers of numbers.

entry.title: Solving Ax = b by undoing a transformation
entry.summary: A linear system asks which vector a matrix sends to b. That view explains when there is one solution, none or a whole line, and what the inverse matrix does.

entry.title: Surfaces and contour maps: functions of two variables
entry.summary: A hiking map shows a mountain on flat paper. Its contour lines are the level sets of a function of two variables, and their spacing measures steepness.

entry.title: The gradient: which way is uphill?
entry.summary: On a hillside the slope depends on the direction you face. Partial derivatives give two of those slopes, and the gradient packs all of them into one arrow.

entry.title: Lagrange multipliers: the best point on a path
entry.summary: The highest point of a trail is where the trail just touches a contour line. There the gradients of the height and of the constraint are parallel.

entry.title: Double integrals: volume under a surface
entry.summary: Volume under a surface is a limit of sums of thin columns. Slicing turns it into two ordinary integrals, and polar coordinates handle round regions.

entry.title: Divergence and curl: reading a vector field
entry.summary: Two numbers at each point of a flow. Divergence is the net outflow from a tiny square per unit area, and curl is the circulation around it per unit area.

entry.title: Green's theorem: the inside read from the boundary
entry.summary: A walk around the edge of a region, adding up a vector field along the way, equals the integral of the field's curl over the inside. Here is why.

entry.title: What probability means: counting equally likely outcomes
entry.summary: Is a total of 7 with two dice three times as likely as a 12, or six times? Settling it leads to sample spaces, events and the rules every probability obeys.

entry.title: Bayes' rule: why a positive test is usually a false alarm
entry.summary: A 99% accurate test for a rare disease comes back positive, and the chance you are sick is about 9%. Conditional probability and Bayes' theorem explain why.
